{{Short description|Technique for improving the efficiency of estimators in conditional moment models}}
{{Multiple issues|
{{context|date=January 2018}}
{{technical|date=January 2019}}
}}

In [[statistics]] and [[econometrics]], '''optimal instruments''' are a technique for improving the [[efficiency (statistics)|efficiency]] of [[estimator]]s in ''conditional moment models'', a class of [[semiparametric model]]s that generate [[conditional expectation]] functions. To estimate parameters of a conditional moment model, the statistician can derive an [[expected value|expectation]] function (defining "moment conditions") and use the [[generalized method of moments]] (GMM). However, there are infinitely many moment conditions that can be generated from a single model; optimal instruments provide the most efficient moment conditions.

As an example, consider the [[nonlinear regression]] model
:<math>y = f(x, \theta) + u</math>
:<math>E[u\mid x]=0</math>
where {{math|''y''}} is a [[scalar (mathematics)|scalar]] (one-dimensional) [[random variable]], {{math|''x''}} is a [[random vector]] with dimension {{math|''k''}}, and {{math|''θ''}} is a {{math|''k''}}-dimensional [[statistical parameter|parameter]]. The conditional moment restriction <math>E[u\mid x]=0</math> is consistent with infinitely many moment conditions. For example:
:<math>E[ux] = E[u x^2] = E[u x^3] = \dots = 0</math>
More generally, for any vector-valued [[function (mathematics)|function]] {{math|''z''}} of {{math|''x''}}, it will be the case that
:<math>E[z(x) (y - f(x, \theta))] = 0</math>.
That is, {{math|''z''}} defines a finite set of [[orthogonality#Statistics, econometrics, and economics|orthogonality]] conditions.

A natural question to ask, then, is whether an [[Efficiency (statistics)#Asymptotic efficiency|asymptotically efficient]] set of conditions is available, in the sense that no other set of conditions achieves lower [[asymptotic variance]].<ref name="Arellano">{{cite web |last=Arellano |first=M. |author-link=Manuel Arellano |year=2009 |title=Generalized Method of Moments and Optimal Instruments |work=Class notes |url=https://www.cemfi.es/~arellano/gmm-estimation.pdf }}</ref> Both econometricians<ref>{{cite journal |last=Chamberlain |first=G. |author-link=Gary Chamberlain |year=1987 |title=Asymptotic Efficiency in Estimation with Conditional Moment Restrictions |journal=[[Journal of Econometrics]] |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=305–334 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(87)90015-7 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Newey |first=W. K. |author-link=Whitney K. Newey |year=1988 |title=Adaptive Estimation of Regression Models via Moment Restrictions |journal=Journal of Econometrics |volume=38 |issue=3 |pages=301–339 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(88)90048-6 }}</ref> and statisticians<ref>{{cite journal |last=Liang |first=K-Y. |first2=S. L. |last2=Zeger |year=1986 |title=Longitudinal Data Analysis using Generalized Linear Models |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=73 |issue=1 |pages=13–22 |doi=10.1093/biomet/73.1.13 |doi-access=free }}</ref> have extensively studied this subject.

The answer to this question is generally that this finite set exists and have been proven for a wide range of estimators. [[Takeshi Amemiya]] was one of the first to work on this problem and show the optimal number of instruments for nonlinear [[simultaneous equation models]] with homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated errors.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Amemiya |first=T. |year=1977 |title=The Maximum Likelihood and the Nonlinear Three-Stage Least Squares Estimator in the General Nonlinear Simultaneous Equation Model |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=955–968 |doi=10.2307/1912684 |jstor=1912684 }}</ref> The form of the optimal instruments was characterized by [[Lars Peter Hansen]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hansen |first=L. P. |year=1985 |title=A Method of Calculating Bounds on the Asymptotic Covariance Matrices of Generalized Method of Moments Estimators |journal=Journal of Econometrics |volume=30 |issue=1–2 |pages=203–238 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(85)90138-1 }}</ref> and results for nonparametric estimation of optimal instruments are provided by Newey.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Newey |first=W. K. |year=1990 |title=Efficient Instrumental Variables Estimation of Nonlinear Models |journal=Econometrica |volume=58 |issue=4 |pages=809–837 |doi=10.2307/2938351 |jstor=2938351 }}</ref> A result for nearest neighbor estimators was provided by Robinson.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Robinson |first=P. |year=1987 |title=Asymptotically Efficient Estimation in the Presence of Heteroskedasticity of Unknown Form |journal=Econometrica |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=875–891 |doi=10.2307/1911033 |jstor=1911033 }}</ref>

== In linear regression ==
The technique of optimal instruments can be used to show that, in a conditional moment [[linear regression]] model with ''[[iid]]'' data, the optimal GMM estimator is [[generalized least squares]]. Consider the model
:<math>y = x^\mathrm T \theta + u</math>
:<math>E[u \mid x] = 0</math>
where {{math|''y''}} is a scalar random variable, {{math|''x''}} is a {{math|''k''}}-dimensional random vector, and {{math|''θ''}} is a {{math|''k''}}-dimensional parameter vector. As above, the moment conditions are
:<math>E[z(x) (y - x^\mathrm T \theta)] = 0</math>
where {{math|''z'' {{=}} ''z''(''x'')}} is an instrument set of dimension {{math|''p''}} ({{math|''p'' ≥ ''k''}}). The task is to choose {{math|''z''}} to minimize the asymptotic variance of the resulting GMM estimator. If the data are ''iid'', the asymptotic variance of the GMM estimator is
:<math>(E[x z^\mathrm T]^\mathrm T E[\sigma^2(x) z z^\mathrm T]^{-1} E[z x^\mathrm T])^{-1}</math>
where <math>\sigma^2(x) \equiv E[u^2 \mid x]</math>.

The optimal instruments are given by
:<math>z^*(x) = \frac{x}{\sigma^2(x)}</math>
which produces the asymptotic variance matrix
:<math>\left( E \left[ \frac{x x^\mathrm T}{\sigma^2(x)} \right] \right)^{-1}.</math>
These are the optimal instruments because for any other {{math|''z''}}, the matrix
:<math>\left( E \left[ \frac{x x^\mathrm T}{\sigma^2(x)} \right] \right)^{-1} - (E[x z^\mathrm T]^\mathrm T E[\sigma^2(x) z z^\mathrm T]^{-1} E[z x^\mathrm T])^{-1}</math>
is [[positive semidefinite matrix|positive semidefinite]].

Given ''iid'' data <math>(y_1, x_1), \dots, (y_N, x_N)</math>, the GMM estimator corresponding to <math>z^*(x)</math> is
:<math>\widetilde\theta = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{x_i x_i^\mathrm T}{\sigma^2(x_i)} \right)^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{x_i y_i}{\sigma^2(x_i)}</math>
which is the generalized least squares estimator. (It is unfeasible because {{math|''σ''<sup>2</sup>(·)}} is unknown.)<ref name="Arellano"/>
